# deepresearch-arms-lab

deepresearch-arms-lab is a 14-arm ablation study on deep-research pipeline design that measures which prompt and pipeline mechanisms actually reduce citation fabrication on a weak base model, for engineers building autonomous research agents.

## What it is

The study asks one question: can a weak Chinese base model write a good research report *and* avoid fabricating citations when doing deep research — autonomous search followed by report writing? To answer it, fourteen prompt and pipeline designs were implemented as runnable code and put through one shared evaluation harness: blind judging by Claude Opus 4.8 on a RACE-style four-dimension rubric (median of 3 samples, 0–10) for quality, and fact-v2 clause-level support rate (0–1) for faithfulness, which re-fetches every cited page and checks whether it actually supports the clause. Fairness controls are the point of the design: every arm runs on the same base model (MiMo 2.5 Pro) and the same search backend behind one wrapper with the agents' built-in web tools disabled, and arms drew subsets of one shared question bank (n=24 / n=10 / n=3, shown beside every figure), with every run writing a trace, a metadata file and the report to disk. The mechanisms tested split into four families — self-discipline during writing (ask nicely, then require a claims ledger), post-hoc citation repair (draft freely, then attach or audit citations against the real tool-call trace), source-side pre-citation (the tool assigns each fetched page a number, the model may only cite numbers, and code turns numbers into footnotes so a URL cannot be fabricated), and research/writing separation (a research pass takes notes, a writing pass drafts from the notes with no search tools at all, a third pass audits). An external baseline swaps the whole pipeline for GPT-Researcher. Negative results and retracted conclusions are kept in the log rather than edited out, because the project's own thesis is that honesty about gaps beats a smoother-looking number.

## Install

Python 3.12 (the version the CI runs) and four dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alloevil/deepresearch-arms-lab.git
cd deepresearch-arms-lab
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Configure the model gateway. This is a shell script to `source`, not a `.env` file:

```bash
cp env_example.sh env.sh
# edit env.sh: point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN at your own
# Anthropic-compatible gateway. https://api.anthropic.com works with no code changes.
source env.sh
```

Reading the published results needs nothing installed at all — the dashboard has its data inlined, so opening the file works offline:

```bash
open dashboard.html
```

## Quickstart

Run four arms on two questions, then judge and fact-check what came out:

```bash
python3 -m eval.run --arms B,F102,F11,F115 --questions q01,q02 --tag my_run
python3 -m eval.run --judge results/my_run --samples 3
python3 -m eval.run --fact results/my_run --v2 --arms B,F102,F11,F115
```

Rebuild the dashboard from your own run:

```bash
python3 scripts/dash_agg.py
python3 scripts/dash_qa_build.py
python3 scripts/embed_qa_data.py
```

Run the test suite:

```bash
python -m pytest tests -q
```

## Verifiable claims

Machine-readable copy with repro commands: https://alloevil.github.io/deepresearch-arms-lab/claims.json

Judge = Claude Opus 4.8 blind evaluation, median of 3, 0–10 (the harness default in `eval/judge.py`; per-run judge metadata stays in the unpublished `results/` tree). Faithfulness = fact-v2 clause-level support rate, 0–1. Baseline **B** is bare execution with no citation machinery. Deltas are within-batch; absolute scores must not be compared across batches, because judge scores drift.

| Claim | Value | n | How measured | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F115 (research → offline writing → audit) costs judged quality against the bare baseline | judge 7.77 vs 7.85, **−0.08** | 24 | same model, backend and questions; reports anonymised and shuffled before judging | `EXPERIMENTS.md` |
| …and buys the second-largest faithfulness gain among the n=24 arms | 0.66 vs 0.42, **+0.24** | 24 | fact-v2 re-fetches each cited page and checks the clause | `EXPERIMENTS.md` |
| F11 (source-side pre-citation) buys the largest faithfulness gain among the n=24 arms and pays the largest quality cost | judge **−0.26**, faithfulness **+0.26** (7.59 / 0.68) | 24 | the model can only cite tool-assigned page numbers; code writes the URLs | `arms/arm_f11_precite.py` |
| F10.2 (independent post-hoc verification of what B wrote) is the lighter-touch option | judge **−0.26**, faithfulness **+0.12** (7.59 / 0.54) | 24 | second pass decides keep / weaken / replace / flag-unverified per citation | `arms/arm_f102_postverify.py` |
| The headline advantage collapsed as the question set grew — no single figure describes it | **+0.66 → +0.12 → −0.08** | 10 → 15 → 24 | same arms re-run at each expansion; 5 deliberately data-rich "hard" questions were added at the end specifically to test whether the effect was a soft-topic artefact. It was not. | `EXPERIMENTS.md` |
| Negative result: a key-claims registry maintained during writing gives no faithfulness gain over just prompting a citation protocol | **0.48 vs 0.48**, per-question latency about 3× the bare baseline's (1217 s vs 404 s on the same 10 questions; 1.3× B3's) | 10 | F9.1 vs B3, paired, same batch | `f91-vs-b3-report.md` |
| Boundary: forcing one atomic claim per sentence on top of pre-citation *reduced* faithfulness | 0.55 vs F11's 0.78 on the same 3 questions, **−0.23** | 3 | F11.3 vs F11; more, weaker-grounded micro-claims | `arms/arm_f113_atomic.py` |
| Preliminary: a mature external framework did not transfer to the weak base model | judge **5.75**, faithfulness **0.45** | 3 | GPT-Researcher, same base model, same backend as far as practical | `arms/arm_g_gptr.py` |
| Every arm is committed runnable code, not a described configuration | **31** files | — | 14 with committed per-question results (all 14 in the dashboard, all 14 tabled or listed in the README), 17 superseded arms kept for the record | `arms/` |

Deliberately **not** claimed: no token or cost figure. The gateway returned no usage block this round, so the `tokens.in/out` fields in the run metadata are 0 and wall-clock `avg_secs` is the only cost proxy available — the harness does read and store usage when the gateway provides it (`common/core.py`, `eval/run.py`), and `meta.json` itself is not published. "Is the extra stage worth it?" can only be answered on latency, not spend.

## When to use it

- You are choosing a citation strategy for a research agent and want measured trade-offs rather than plausible-sounding advice — specifically, how much judged quality each faithfulness mechanism costs.
- You are working with a weak or small base model and need to know which mechanisms survive that. Several that sound reasonable do not: asking for a protocol, requiring a ledger, allowing an uncited "background knowledge" channel.
- You want a worked example of an evaluation harness with real controls: one search backend behind a wrapper, agents' built-in web tools disabled, blind anonymised shuffled judging, median-of-3 with dispersion reported, a closed-book baseline to separate retrieval gain from parametric knowledge, and a contamination audit.
- You want to read a study that documents its own retractions. The "dual-optimal winner" claim, the +0.66 headline, and a mis-recorded win/loss tally are all visible in the log with the correction next to them.
- You want the raw per-question artefacts — question, full report, scoring rationale — to inspect rather than a summary table.

## When NOT to use it

- **You want a recommendation to copy.** There isn't one. At n=24 all three structural arms score below the bare baseline on judged quality; which you should pick depends on whether your use case weights "reads complete" or "everything said is grounded". The project explicitly withdrew its earlier single-winner framing.
- **You want numbers that generalise to a strong model.** Everything here is measured on one weak base model (MiMo 2.5 Pro). Several findings are specifically about weak-model failure modes; do not assume they hold for a frontier model.
- **You want cost or token comparisons.** No figures available: the gateway returned no usage block, so `tokens.in/out` are 0 for this round and only wall-clock latency is available.
- **You want statistical significance.** Judge scores vary run-to-run by about 1.0 on the same prompt, measured empirically. The n=10 Hybrid-v6 comparison reported a paired bootstrap 95% CI of [−0.06, +0.21] around a +0.09 mean difference — crossing zero, and the log estimates n≈60 would be needed to detect an effect that size. Read every number next to its `n`; three arms are at n=3 and labelled exploratory.
- **You expect the headline numbers to be stable.** They are not, and the study says so: the same comparison moved 0.74 points as the question set grew from 10 to 24 questions. Expect further movement as the set grows.
- **You want English-language content.** The experiment log, reports and survey notes are in Chinese; the README is bilingual. The questions are Chinese research topics, so retrieval quality is entangled with the Chinese-language web.
- **You need faithfulness measured on academic citations.** fact-v2 verifies by fetching the cited page, so `Author, "Title," Venue, Year` citations with no URL score zero checkable pairs. On one question two arms were therefore simply unmeasured. This is disclosed as a known blind spot in the ruler, not patched around.

## Compared to GPT-Researcher

GPT-Researcher is the one named external alternative the study actually ran, as arm G: the whole pipeline replaced by that framework, pointed at the same base model and, as far as practical, the same search backend. It scored judge 5.75 and faithfulness 0.45 at n=3, below every custom arm including the bare baseline. The stated reading is deliberately narrow — search-quota and embedding-language problems made a larger batch impractical, so this is a preliminary signal, not proof that external frameworks cannot work here. What it does support is the weaker and more useful claim: a leaderboard-strong pipeline's advantage does not automatically transfer across a change of model, language and retrieval source.

The survey files compare *designs* rather than running the systems. Their finding is that no mainstream system relies on the model voluntarily obeying a citation protocol while writing: the training-oriented camp (OpenAI, Kimi) internalises it with format and rubric rewards, while the orchestration camp (Anthropic, Gemini, Perplexity, and every open-source framework) makes citation a pipeline structure — a post-hoc CitationAgent, collection-side source tracking, or provenance pre-bound at the retrieval layer. That is precisely the path F9.1 tried and the path the industry avoids, which is consistent with F9.1's null result here. Two further design comparisons are recorded with sources: LangChain reported that parallel section-writing produced disjointed reports and converged on "research in parallel, write in one pass", while STORM and GPT-Researcher × Deep Agents keep section-writing but add a global constraint layer (outline-first, or a chief editor that reviews and sends drafts back) — so the strength of the coordination layer sets how much freedom the writing stage can have.

## FAQ

**What is the single most important finding?**
That structural mechanisms reliably buy citation faithfulness and reliably cost judged quality, with no dual-optimal option at n=24. F115 trades 0.08 judge points for 0.24 faithfulness, F11 trades 0.26 for 0.26, F10.2 trades 0.26 for 0.12. The mechanism behind the cost is explainable and reproducible rather than noise: pipelines that refuse to write what they could not retrieve produce honest blanks, and both the LLM judge and most human readers penalise an honest blank more than a smooth, confident, unsupported paragraph.

**Why keep negative results and superseded conclusions in the log?**
Because the study is about faithfulness, and silently editing a retracted number out would be the same failure it measures. The log therefore contains, with corrections attached: the +0.66 headline that became −0.08, the "dual-optimal winner" framing that was withdrawn at n=20, a win/loss tally that was mis-recorded and corrected against the score files, an F9.1 protocol that produced no gain, three F11 perturbations that all failed, and a search-quota exhaustion incident that turned into a finding — evidence-gated systems failed loudly ("cannot write, no evidence") and scored 4–6, agent-style systems failed silently by substituting parametric knowledge and scored 7–8, and the judge could not detect zero-evidence fabrication.

**How does source-side pre-citation prevent fabricated URLs?**
The search and read tools are wrapped so every fetched page is given a stable numeric id, injected into a header the model sees. The writing rule is then mechanical: you may only cite a page you were assigned a number for, and you write the number, never a URL. A post-processing step converts each number into a real footnote with the URL filled in by code. The model never writes a URL, so it structurally cannot invent one. The measured cost is 0.26 judge points at n=24, plus a real failure mode: on one multi-page comparison question the per-page numbering overhead pushed the drafting stage into a 60-turn ceiling twice in independent retries, and the question was removed from the set rather than raising the limit for one arm.

**Can I trust the absolute scores?**
No, and you are not asked to. Judge scores drift by roughly 1.0 run-to-run on the same prompt, and swapping in a date-injected judge prompt shifted arm scores by 0.3–0.6. Only same-batch, same-judge comparisons are meaningful, which is why every table carries its `n` and why the log repeatedly warns against cross-table comparison of absolutes. Three arms are at n=3 and marked exploratory; the four main arms are at n=24.

**Where do the questions come from, and is contamination handled?**
Ten questions are the project's own Chinese research topics in `eval/questions.json`. The n=24 comparison uses 14 questions borrowed verbatim from DeepResearch Bench (Apache-2.0), attributed in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`. Contamination is audited by `eval/contamination.py` on two offline levels (BML/QCL); the third level it documents (EAL) needs page fetches plus an LLM and is out of scope there. A closed-book baseline (`run.py --no-search`) runs the same questions with retrieval disabled so that the open-book minus closed-book difference isolates the actual retrieval gain rather than the model's parametric knowledge.
